citations.quote: For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.
Assume countable choice. If $f\in L^1\cap L^2$, its bounded continuous integral transform $\widehat f$ represents $\mathcal F_2f$ almost everywhere.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the
proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice and the
Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the transverse
subspace
$$\mathfrak h:=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):\ k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{for a.e. }k\Bigr\}$$
with the $L^2$ inner product, define the bounded multiplier-valued function
$\Pi(k):=\mathrm{id}-|k|^{-2}kk^{\mathsf T}$ for $k\ne0$ and $\Pi(0):=0$, and let
$M_\Pi$ be multiplication by $\Pi$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Write
$\varepsilon(k):=\alpha|k|$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be multiplication by
$\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}:=M_\varepsilon|_{\mathfrak h}$.
Let $F(\mathfrak h)$ be the Fock space of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] with sectors
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and for $n\ge1$ define
$$T_n\psi:=\varepsilon_n\psi,\quad \varepsilon_n(k_1,\dots,k_n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha|k_i|,\qquad D(T_n):=\{\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}:\varepsilon_n\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\},$$
and $T_0:=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Finally put
$$H_f:=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T_n,\qquad D(H_f):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(\mathfrak h):\ \sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$
Then:

(a) $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed separable subspace of
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, invariant under $M_\varepsilon$, and
$\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on
$\mathfrak h$ with $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]],
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]);

(b) each $T_n$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with the displayed domain
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]],
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]);

(c) $H_f$ is self-adjoint and positive with domain $D(H_f)$; it commutes with
every sector projection $\Pi_n$ (i.e. $T_n$ maps its sector into itself);

(d) for every $\beta>0$ the bounded operator $e^{-\beta H_f}$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]) is not compact and in particular not trace
class ([[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]); more
precisely its restriction to the one-particle sector equals the multiplication
operator $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$, which is not compact, and
the restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact.

The identification of $\mathfrak h$, $\varepsilon$ and $H_f$ with physical
transverse photons in a chosen frame is a separate model assumption and is not
asserted here; no thermal interpretation of $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is claimed either.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\alpha>0$, let
$\mathfrak h$ be the transverse space and $H_f=\bigoplus_nT_n$ the free
transverse Fock Hamiltonian of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]],
and let $A_\pm(g)$, $g\in\mathfrak h$, be the maximal creation and annihilation
operators on $F(\mathfrak h)$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]]. Fix a cutoff
$\Lambda>0$ and vectors $g_1,\dots,g_J\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) with
$$\operatorname{supp}g_j\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\}\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{g_j}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h,\qquad \varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|,$$
and define the symmetric operator
$$\phi(g):=A_-(g)+A_+(g),\qquad D(\phi(g)):=D(H_f).$$
Let $d\ge1$, let $H_a$ be a Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix, and let
$D_1,\dots,D_J$ be Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices with operator norms
$\|D_j\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). Then:

(a) for every $\Psi\in D(H_f)$,
$$\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2\le\Bigl\|\frac g{\sqrt\varepsilon}\Bigr\|^2\langle H_f\Psi,\Psi\rangle,\qquad
\|A_+(g)\Psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\Psi\|^2;$$
in particular $\Psi\in D(A_+(g))\cap D(A_-(g))$ and for every $\eta>0$ there is
a finite $C_\eta$ with
$$\|\phi(g)\Psi\|\le\eta\|H_f\Psi\|+C_\eta\|\Psi\| ;$$

(b) $\phi(g)$ is symmetric on $D(H_f)$ and has $H_f$-bound zero
([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(c) the free part $H_0:=H_a\otimes I+I\otimes H_f$ with domain
$C^d\otimes D(H_f)$ is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$
([[def-hilbert-space]]); for every $\eta_0\in\mathbb R$ the operator
$$H:=H_0+\eta_0\sum_{j=1}^JD_j\otimes\phi(g_j),\qquad D(H):=C^d\otimes D(H_f),$$
is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$ and bounded below
([[thm-kato-rellich]],
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]] (c)).

The product $D_j\otimes\phi(g_j)$ and the coupling $\eta_0$ carry the dimension
of energy in a physical normalisation; this normalisation is a model choice and
no physical statement about radiation or spontaneous emission is made here.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Throughout, $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are **abbreviations and not real numbers**,
exactly as in [[def-interval]] and [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]. Every phrase
below is a single abbreviation for a displayed condition on reals, and no
arithmetic is ever performed with the symbols.

**Limits at $+\infty$.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be **not bounded above**
([[def-bounded-set]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. We
write

$$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$$

when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $M$ such that

$$|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for every } x \in A \text{ with } x > M .$$

**Limits at $-\infty$.** Let $A$ be **not bounded below**. We write
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L$ when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a
real $M$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in A$ with $x < M$.

**Why unboundedness is required.** It plays exactly the role the limit-point
condition plays in [[def-function-limit]]. Saying that $A$ is not bounded above
says that no real is an upper bound of $A$, that is, that for every real $M$
there is $x \in A$ with $x > M$ ([[def-bounded-set]],
[[def-complete-ordered-field]]); so the set over which the condition quantifies
is never empty and the condition is never vacuous. Without the hypothesis every
real $L$ would satisfy it and the notation would not denote.

**Uniqueness, proved here.** Suppose $A$ is not bounded above and
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L'$ with
$L \ne L'$. Then $|L - L'| > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), so
$\varepsilon := |L - L'|/2 > 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]],
[[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]). Choose reals $M_1, M_2$
witnessing the two conditions at this $\varepsilon$ and let $M$ be the larger of
them, the order being total. Since $A$ is not bounded above there is $x \in A$
with $x > M$, hence with $x > M_1$ and $x > M_2$, and then

$$|L - L'| = |(L - f(x)) + (f(x) - L')| \le |f(x) - L| + |f(x) - L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L - L'|$$

([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-add-order]]),
which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$, and the notation
$\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)$ denotes a single real. The same four lines, with the
inequalities on $x$ reversed, give uniqueness at $-\infty$.

**Infinite limits at a point.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We write

$$f(x) \to +\infty \ \text{ as } \ x \to c$$

when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $f(x) > M$ for
every $x \in A$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$; and $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to c$
when for every real $M$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $f(x) < M$ for every
such $x$.

**This library does not write $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = +\infty$.** The right-hand
side would not be an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and writing the equation would
silently move the discussion into the extended real line, a structure that is
not a field. That is the convention already fixed by
[[def-divergence-to-infinity]] for sequences and by [[rem-sup-conventions]] for
suprema, and it is kept here. In particular none of the rules of
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]] may be applied to a function tending to
$\pm\infty$.

**Combined forms.** Let $A$ be not bounded above and $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$. We
write $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to +\infty$ when for every real $N$ there is a
real $M$ with $f(x) > N$ for every $x \in A$ with $x > M$. The other forms are
obtained the same way, by pairing one of the two conditions on $x$ (unbounded
above, unbounded below) with one of the two conditions on $f(x)$ (above every
real, below every real); each is again a single abbreviation for the displayed
condition, and none of them is an equation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $V$ be a normed space. A **sequence in $V$** is a function
$x:\mathbb N\to V$, written $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_n:=x(n)$
([[def-natural-numbers]]). Fix such a sequence.

Define its vector partial sums recursively by

$$s_0:=0_V,\qquad s_{m+1}:=s_m+x_m.$$

We write $s_m=\sum_{n<m}x_n$. The **series**
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty x_n$ **converges** when these partial sums converge in $V$.
Its sum is then the limit of the partial sums.

The series is **absolutely convergent** when the scalar series
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \|x_n\|$$
converges in the sense of [[def-series]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space, let $\mathcal{B}$ be a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) and let $A \subseteq X$. Interior
and closure are as in [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]].

- $A$ is **dense** in $X$ if $\overline{A} = X$.
- $A$ is **codense** in $X$ if $X \setminus A$ is dense.
- $A$ is **nowhere dense** in $X$ if $\operatorname{int}(\overline{A}) = \varnothing$.

**Three equivalent forms of density, and the one used in practice.** The
following are equivalent:

1. $\overline{A} = X$;
2. $U \cap A \ne \varnothing$ for every nonempty open $U \subseteq X$;
3. $B \cap A \ne \varnothing$ for every nonempty $B \in \mathcal{B}$.

*Proof.* (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): if $U$ is open and nonempty, pick $x \in U$; then
$x \in \overline{A}$, so $U \cap A \ne \varnothing$ by clause (c) of
[[thm-closure-characterisation-top]]. (2) $\Rightarrow$ (3): a nonempty member of
$\mathcal{B}$ is a nonempty open set. (3) $\Rightarrow$ (1): let $x \in X$; every
$B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B$ is nonempty and so meets $A$, hence
$x \in \overline{A}$ by clause (d) of [[thm-closure-characterisation-top]]. Form
3 is what makes density checkable: for the Sorgenfrey line it is a statement
about half-open intervals, and for a metric space a statement about balls.

**Codensity is emptiness of the interior.** $A$ is codense if and only if
$\operatorname{int}(A) = \varnothing$, because
$X \setminus \operatorname{int}(A) = \overline{X \setminus A}$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]), so $\overline{X \setminus A} = X$ holds
exactly when $\operatorname{int}(A) = \varnothing$.

**Nowhere dense implies codense, and the converse fails.** If
$\operatorname{int}(\overline{A}) = \varnothing$ then
$\operatorname{int}(A) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(\overline{A}) = \varnothing$
by monotonicity of the interior, so $A$ is codense. The two notions can differ
only on sets whose closure is larger than themselves, and there they sometimes
do: a dense set with empty interior, such as the rationals inside the real line,
is codense and is not nowhere dense, its closure being everything. They may also
agree on such a set: $(0,1)$ inside $\mathbb{R}$ has closure $[0,1]$ and is
neither codense nor nowhere dense. A *closed* set is nowhere dense
precisely when it is codense, since then $\overline{A} = A$.

derivations.claim: [Absolutely convergent pairing] Let $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$. By [F2] with $a_n:=\|\psi_n\|$, $b_n:=\|\varphi_n\|$, $\sum_n|\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle|\le\sum_n\|\psi_n\|\,\|\varphi_n\|\le\bigl(\sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_n\|\varphi_n\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\|\psi\|\,\|\varphi\|<\infty$, so the series defining $\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle$ converges absolutely ([[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]); the value is unchanged by rearranging each term, and termwise addition and scalar multiplication give sesquilinearity and linearity in the first argument, inherited from the pairings on the $H^{\otimes n}$. If $\|\psi\|^2=\sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2=0$ then $\psi_n=0$ for every $n$, so $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with the displayed inner product.

[Completeness] Let $(\psi^{(k)})_k$ be a Cauchy sequence in $F(H)$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. For each $n$, $\|\psi_n^{(k)}-\psi_n^{(l)}\|\le\|\psi^{(k)}-\psi^{(l)}\|$, so $(\psi_n^{(k)})_k$ is Cauchy in the complete space $H^{\otimes n}$ ([F1]) and converges to some $\psi_n\in H^{\otimes n}$; since $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is closed, $\psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ ([F1]). Choose $K$ with $\|\psi^{(k)}-\psi^{(m)}\|\le\varepsilon$ for $k,m\ge K$; for every finite $N$ and $k,m\ge K$, $\sum_{n\le N}\|\psi_n^{(k)}-\psi_n^{(m)}\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$, and letting $m\to\infty$ gives $\sum_{n\le N}\|\psi_n^{(k)}-\psi_n\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ for every $N$, hence $\|\psi^{(k)}-\psi\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$. In particular $\psi\in F(H)$ and $\psi^{(k)}\to\psi$; thus $F(H)$ is complete and (b) holds.

[Vacuum, density and embeddings] The vacuum has $\|\Omega\|=|1|=1$. For $\psi\in F(H)$ the truncations $\psi^{(N)}:=(\psi_0,\dots,\psi_N,0,0,\dots)\in F_0$ satisfy $\|\psi-\psi^{(N)}\|^2=\sum_{n>N}\|\psi_n\|^2\to0$, so $F_0$ is dense by [F4]; $F_0$ is a linear subspace because each $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is one ([F1]). Each $\iota_n$ is linear and $\|\iota_n(u)\|^2=\|u\|^2$, and its range is the set of vectors supported in coordinate $n$, a closed subspace identified isometrically with $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$.

[The direct sum is closed] Let $(T_n)$ be as in (f) and let $(\psi^{(k)})_k\subseteq D(T)$ with $\psi^{(k)}\to\psi$ and $T\psi^{(k)}\to\eta$ in $F(H)$. For each $n$, $\psi_n^{(k)}\to\psi_n$ and $T_n\psi_n^{(k)}=(T\psi^{(k)})_n\to\eta_n$; since $T_n$ is self-adjoint, hence closed ([F3]), $\psi_n\in D(T_n)$ and $T_n\psi_n=\eta_n$. Since $\|T_n\psi_n\|^2=\lim_k\|T_n\psi_n^{(k)}\|^2$ for each $n$, Fatou's lemma for series gives $\sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2\le\liminf_k\sum_n\|T_n\psi_n^{(k)}\|^2=\liminf_k\|T\psi^{(k)}\|^2<\infty$, so $\psi\in D(T)$ and $T\psi=\eta$; thus $T$ is closed. It is symmetric because for $\psi,\varphi\in D(T)$ the middle series below converges absolutely by [F2] applied to the square-summable families $(\|T_n\psi_n\|)_n$, $(\varphi_n)_n$ and $(\|T_n\varphi_n\|)_n$: $\langle T\psi,\varphi\rangle=\sum_n\langle T_n\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle=\sum_n\langle\psi_n,T_n\varphi_n\rangle=\langle\psi,T\varphi\rangle$.

[Separability] Assume $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $H$ with $I$ at most countable. For $n\ge1$ the elementary tensors $e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$, $(i_1,\dots,i_n)\in I^n$, have dense linear span in $H^{\otimes n}$ by the product-bases statement of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]; since $P_+^{(n)}$ is bounded, the image $P_+^{(n)}$ of a dense set is dense in $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ (given $u=P_+^{(n)}u$ in the range and approximants $v_j\to u$, continuity gives $P_+^{(n)}v_j\to u$). Hence the at most countable set $D:=\{\iota_n(P_+^{(n)}(e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n})):n\ge1,\ i_1,\dots,i_n\in I\}\cup\{\Omega\}$ has dense span in $F(H)$: any $\psi\in F(H)$ is the limit of its truncations, and each $\psi_n$ is approximated in $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ by finite combinations from $D$. A normed space with a countable set whose finite linear combinations are dense is separable.

[The adjoint is the same diagonal sum] Let $\varphi\in D(T^*)$ with $C:=\|T^*\varphi\|$, so $|\langle T\psi,\varphi\rangle|\le C\|\psi\|$ for all $\psi\in D(T)$. Testing with $\psi$ supported in a single coordinate $n$ shows that the functional $\psi_n\mapsto\langle T_n\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ on the dense domain $D(T_n)$ is bounded by $C\|\psi_n\|$; hence $\varphi_n\in D(T_n^*)=D(T_n)$ and $T_n\varphi_n=(T^*\varphi)_n$. For every finite set $F$ of coordinates and reals $\lambda_n\ge0$, take unit vectors $\chi_n\in D(T_n)$ with $\operatorname{Re}\langle\chi_n,T_n\varphi_n\rangle\ge\|T_n\varphi_n\|-\delta$ (density of $D(T_n)$) and put $\psi:=\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_n\chi_n$; then $\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_n\|T_n\varphi_n\|\le|\langle T\psi,\varphi\rangle|+\delta\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_n\le C\bigl(\sum_{n\in F}\lambda_n^2\bigr)^{1/2}+\delta\,|F|$, and letting $\delta\to0$ and optimising over finitely supported $(\lambda_n)$ gives $\sum_n\|T_n\varphi_n\|^2\le C^2<\infty$. Therefore $D(T^*)\subseteq D(T)$ and $T^*\varphi=T\varphi$; with $T\subseteq T^*$ from step 1.4, $T=T^*$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense (it contains $F_0$). If every $T_n$ is bounded by $M:=\sup_n\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $\|T\psi\|^2=\sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2\le M^2\|\psi\|^2$ for every $\psi\in F(H)$ and testing on a unit vector in a single coordinate where $\|T_n\|$ is nearly $M$ gives the reverse inequality.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let
$H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor
powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let
$P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set
$P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for
its range and define

$$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$

Then:

(a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series
$\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and
defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to
which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$
([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]],
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]);

(b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm
is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]);

(c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the
finite-particle space
$F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense
linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]);

(d) for every $n$ the map
$\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$,
$\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear
isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors
supported in coordinate $n$;

(e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]);

(f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\ge 1$ a self-adjoint
operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain
$D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and

$$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$

then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is
bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with
$\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum
operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$.

\|S_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1.$$

for all $f\in H$ and $\varphi,\psi\in F_0$
([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

(d) *Canonical commutation relation.* For all $f,g\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$,
$$S_-(f)S_+(g)\psi-S_+(g)S_-(f)\psi=\langle g,f\rangle\,\psi,$$
and consequently
$$\|S_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|S_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2.$$

Neither $S_+(f)$ nor $S_-(f)$ is asserted to be bounded on $F(H)$, and no
physical interpretation (particle creation, radiation or measurement) is
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let
$H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor
powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let
$P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set
$P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for
its range and define

$$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$

Then:

(a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series
$\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and
defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to
which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$
([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]],
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]);

(b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm
is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]);

(c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the
finite-particle space
$F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense
linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]);

(d) for every $n$ the map
$\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$,
$\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear
isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors
supported in coordinate $n$;

(e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]);

(f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\ge 1$ a self-adjoint
operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain
$D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and

$$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$

then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is
bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with
$\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum
operators is asserted.

derivations.claim: [Self-adjointness and positivity] For every $n\ge1$ the operator $T_n:=n\,\mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}}$ is bounded self-adjoint on the Hilbert space $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and $T_0=0$ on $\mathbb C$; its domain condition $\sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ reads exactly $\sum_nn^2\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$. By [F2] the direct sum $N=\bigoplus_nT_n$ is self-adjoint and densely defined on the displayed domain, and for $\psi\in D(N)$, $\langle N\psi,\psi\rangle=\sum_nn\|\psi_n\|^2\ge0$. The vacuum has $N\Omega=0$, and the truncations $\psi^{(N)}$ lie in $F_0$, satisfy $\psi^{(N)}\to\psi$ and $N\psi^{(N)}\to N\psi$ by convergence of $\sum_nn^2\|\psi_n\|^2$; hence $F_0$ is a core.

[Commutation on the core] Let $f\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$; all vectors below lie in $F_0$ by [F3]. Using the sector formulas of [F3], for $n\ge1$ the $n$-th coordinate of $S_+(f)N\psi$ is $\sqrt nP_+^{(n)}(f\otimes(n-1)\psi_{n-1})=(n-1)(S_+(f)\psi)_n$, while the $n$-th coordinate of $NS_+(f)\psi$ is $n(S_+(f)\psi)_n$; both coordinates vanish for $n=0$. Hence $NS_+(f)\psi-S_+(f)N\psi=S_+(f)\psi$. Similarly, the $n$-th coordinate of $S_-(f)N\psi$ is $\sqrt{n+1}\Psi_f^{(n)}((n+1)\psi_{n+1})=(n+1)(S_-(f)\psi)_n$, and that of $NS_-(f)\psi$ is $n(S_-(f)\psi)_n$; their difference is $-(S_-(f)\psi)_n$ for every $n$, proving the second identity.

[Eigenvalues and spectrum] Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $u\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, $u
e0$. The vector $\iota_n(u)$ lies in $D(N)$ with $(N\iota_n(u))_m=m(\iota_n(u))_m$, which is $n\iota_n(u)$. For $\lambda
otin\mathbb N$ the direct sum $ igoplus_n(n-\lambda)^{-1}I_n$ has $\sup_n|n-\lambda|^{-1}<\infty$ (because $|n-\lambda|\ge\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\mathbb N)>0$) and is therefore, by [F4], a bounded inverse of $N-\lambda I$; hence $\lambda
otin\sigma(N)$ and $\sigma(N)\subseteq\mathbb N$, while the eigenvalues exhibited give $\mathbb N\subseteq\sigma(N)$, so $\sigma(N)=\mathbb N$ for $H
e\{0\}$.

[Domain inclusion and moments] If $\psi\in D(N)$ then $\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2=\sum_nn\|\psi_n\|^2+\sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2\le\sum_nn^2\|\psi_n\|^2+\|\psi\|^2<\infty$ (using $n\le n^2$), so $D(N)\subseteq D_1$. The coordinate formula $(N\psi)_n=n\psi_n$ and orthogonality of the sectors give $\|N\psi\|^2=\sum_n\|n\psi_n\|^2=\sum_nn^2\|\psi_n\|^2$ and $\langle N\psi,\psi\rangle=\sum_nn\|\psi_n\|^2$, both series converging absolutely; this proves (d) and completes the proof of (a)-(d).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$ and identify $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$ with Lebesgue measure ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a)$, $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b)$. Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $N\ge1$, let
$m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and $\hbar>0$, write points of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ as
$X=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^3$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the
Plancherel transform of [[thm-plancherel]] with the convention
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(X)e^{-2\pi iX\cdot\xi}\,dX$ on $L^1$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]). Define the quadratic weight and the
free kinetic operator
$$\kappa(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_N):=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_i}|\xi_i|^2,\qquad K:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_\kappa\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(K):=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C):\ \kappa\,\mathcal F_2u\in L^2\}$$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]).
Let $V:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and bounded, with
$\|V\|_\infty:=\operatorname{ess\,sup}|V|<\infty$, and let $M_V$ be
multiplication by $V$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]],
[[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

(a) $K$ is a self-adjoint positive operator with domain $D(K)$, and $D(K)$ is
the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)$ as a set, with
$\|\cdot\|_{W^{2,2}}$ equivalent to the graph norm
$u\mapsto(\|u\|^2+\|Ku\|^2)^{1/2}$
([[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]],
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]);

(b) $H:=K+M_V$ with $D(H):=D(K)$ is self-adjoint and bounded below by
$-\|V\|_\infty$; the space $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)$ is a core for
both $K$ and $H$ ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]],
[[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]);

(c) for every $r\ge1$ the operator $K\otimes I_r+M_V\otimes I_r$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)\otimes\mathbb C^r$, with domain
$D(K)\otimes\mathbb C^r$, is self-adjoint and bounded below by $-\|V\|_\infty$.

In particular, if $V_i:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $W_{ij}:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$
($1\le i<j\le N$) are measurable and bounded and
$V(X):=\sum_iV_i(x_i)+\sum_{i<j}W_{ij}(x_i-x_j)$, then $\|V\|_\infty\le\sum_i\|V_i\|_\infty+\sum_{i<j}\|W_{ij}\|_\infty<\infty$
and (a)-(c) apply. No Hunziker-van Winter-Zhislin threshold statement, no
stability of matter, no thermodynamic-limit and no physical interpretation is
asserted.

derivations.claim: [The averages are projections] Since $\pi\mapsto U_\pi$ is a unitary representation and $U_\pi^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$, $P_+^*=\frac1{N!}\sum_\pi U_{\pi^{-1}}=P_+$ and $P_+^2=\frac1{(N!)^2}\sum_{\pi,\sigma}U_{\pi\sigma}=\frac1{N!}\sum_\tau U_\tau=P_+$; the same computation with the characters gives $P_-^*=P_-$, $P_-^2=P_-$. Hence both are orthogonal projections, which is (a).

[Resolvent commutation] Fix $z\in\rho(H)$ and $\varphi\in\mathfrak H$; put $\psi:=R(z)\varphi\in D(H)$. By hypothesis $U_\pi\psi\in D(H)$ and $(H-z)U_\pi\psi=U_\pi(H-z)\psi=U_\pi\varphi$; hence $U_\pi R(z)\varphi=R(z)U_\pi\varphi$ for every $\varphi$, so $U_\pi R(z)=R(z)U_\pi$; averaging gives $P_\pm R(z)=R(z)P_\pm$, which is (b).

[Reduction] For $\psi\in D(H)$, $P_\pm\psi=\frac1{N!}\sum_\pi U_\pi\psi\in D(H)$ as a finite sum, and $HP_\pm\psi=\frac1{N!}\sum_\pi HU_\pi\psi=\frac1{N!}\sum_\pi U_\pi H\psi=P_\pm H\psi$, which is (c).

[Self-adjointness of the restrictions] Assume $\operatorname{ran}P\ne\{0\}$ for $P=P_\pm$ and put $\mathfrak K:=\operatorname{ran}P$ and $S:=H|_{D(H)\cap\mathfrak K}$. Then $D(S)=P D(H)$ is dense in $\mathfrak K$ and $S$ is symmetric: for $\varphi,\psi\in D(S)$, $\langle S\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle H\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,H\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,S\psi\rangle$ because $H$ is self-adjoint and $\psi=P\psi$. $S$ is closed: if $\psi_k\in D(S)$, $\psi_k\to\psi$ and $S\psi_k\to\eta$ with $\psi,\eta\in\mathfrak K$, then $H$ closed gives $\psi\in D(H)$ and $H\psi=\eta$, and $\psi\in\mathfrak K$ because $\mathfrak K$ is closed; hence $\psi\in D(S)$, $S\psi=\eta$. Finally $\operatorname{ran}(S-i)=P\operatorname{ran}(H-i)$: indeed $(S-i)P\psi=P(H-i)\psi$ by step 1.3, and conversely every $P\chi$ with $\chi\in\mathfrak H$ equals $P(H-i)(H-i)^{-1}\chi=(S-i)P(H-i)^{-1}\chi$. Since $H-i$ is onto $\mathfrak H$ ([F3] applied to the self-adjoint $H$), $\operatorname{ran}(S-i)=\mathfrak K$, and the same argument gives $\operatorname{ran}(S+i)=\mathfrak K$. By [F3], $S$ is self-adjoint on $\mathfrak K$; this proves (d).

[The permutation-invariant instance] Let $H=K+M_V$ as in (e). The unitaries $U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}=\Theta U_\pi\Theta^{-1}$ form a unitary representation of $S_N$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^{3N})$ ([F4]). The weight $\kappa(\xi)=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\sum_i|\xi_i|^2$ is invariant under permutations of the blocks $\xi_i$, so $\Theta U_\pi\Theta^{-1}$ maps $D(K)$ onto itself and intertwines $K$ with itself; and $V(\pi X)=V(X)$ gives $U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}M_VU_\pi^{\mathrm{phys},-1}=M_V$ on all of $L^2$. Hence $U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}D(H)=D(H)$ and $U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}H=HU_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}$ on $D(H)$, and step 2.1 applies to $P_\pm^{\mathrm{phys}}$, proving (e).

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1-3.1 prove (a)-(e). The scope paragraph of the statement records that no spin-statistics assignment and no spectral conclusion is asserted; the symmetric and antisymmetric sectors are mathematical invariant subspaces of the specified operator.
